vignette: The radio crackles over the morning coffee. Karim sets his mug down before it spills, shoulders tight. He is forty now, a paramedic with twelve years on the road, but his hands still remember the weight of his brother's chest that rainy Tuesday. He was off duty, pulling into the driveway, when he sees Tariq's motorcycle crumpled against the stone wall. No sirens yet. Just the heavy silence before the screaming starts. Karim runs. He presses two fingers to Tariq's carotid, finds nothing, and begins compressions. The rhythm becomes a prayer: push, release, push, release. He calls out for his father, counts until his forearms burn, and watches the dark pool spread. By the time the official unit arrives, Tariq's pupils are fixed. The ambulance takes him anyway. The days that follow are a blur of sterile corridors, fluorescent lights, and the slow surrender of hope. Now, Karim rides the same streets, but the city feels different. He sits in his briefing room, listening to the shift supervisor outline today's routes. The air feels thin. He checks his radio twice, then his seatbelt, then the medical bag zippers. His wife, Layla, leaves a folded note in his pocket: Come home for dinner at seven. He reads it three times before the compartment bell rings. When the call goes out-a multi-vehicle collision on the coastal highway-Karim's breath catches. He straps in, starts the engine, and forces his exhale to match the tires. On scene, a young man is trapped under a sedan. Karim works the jaws of life, movements precise, automatic. But beneath the professionalism, his heart hammers. Every time the patient gasps, Karim's throat tightens. He tells himself he is fine. He has saved dozens of lives. Still, when the family arrives, Karim steps back. He cannot watch the reunion. He walks to the edge of the road, watches the street, and feels a hollow ache in his chest. Sleep has become a negotiation. Karim lies awake while Layla sleeps beside him, counting the seconds between her breaths. When she turns over, he tenses. He stops sleeping past midnight. In the mornings, he wakes with a start, convinced he hears a siren. He showers quickly, dresses without looking at himself, and leaves before the house feels heavy. At work, he volunteers for every trauma call. He tells his partner he is clearing his schedule. In truth, he chases the calls like a man chasing a shadow, hoping this time the outcome will be different. He avoids the eastern district where the accident happened. He changes his route, adds ten minutes to his commute, just to keep the intersection out of sight. His partner notices the way Karim scans the crowd before stepping off the rig, the way his gaze lingers on headlights, on raised hands, on any sudden movement. Layla tries to anchor him. She packs extra snacks in his bag, leaves photos on the dashboard, asks him to talk about his day. He does, but the words feel distant. He describes the calls, the protocols, the equipment, but not the part where his hands shake while he writes the report. He does not mention the way he flinches when a child runs toward the curb, or how he counts the exits in every room he enters. He loves his wife fiercely. He kisses her forehead every night, but he cannot remember the last time he slept through the night without dreaming of pavement and the smell of copper. Tonight, the call comes in quiet. A collapsed apartment building. Karim arrives, breathes in the dust, and begins. His boots crunch over rebar. His radio hums. He places a hand on a stranger's shoulder, feels the fragile pulse beneath his glove, and exhales. The night stretches ahead. The city does not slow down. He adjusts his gloves, steps forward, and keeps moving.
